subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Where is the centre for the deglutition (swallowing) reflex located?
back: The Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS) in the medulla

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which cranial nerves are involved in the deglutition reflex?
back: Cranial nerves 5, 9, 10, and 12

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: During swallowing, what does elevation of the soft palate achieve?
back: It closes Passavant's ridge, preventing nasal regurgitation

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: During swallowing, what is the purpose of glottis closure?
back: Airway protection

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: During swallowing, what happens to the upper esophageal sphincter (UES) and why?
back: It relaxes, allowing food to enter the esophagus

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the enterogastric reflex?
back: A reflex in which the duodenum inhibits gastric motility and gastric emptying

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which hormones mediate the enterogastric reflex?
back: Cholecystokinin (CCK), Secretin, and Peptide YY

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Rank the relative stimulus strength of fat, protein, and carbohydrate for the enterogastric reflex
back: Fat > Protein > Carbohydrates

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the two main mediators/triggers of the enterogastric reflex?
back: Duodenal acidity and increased osmolarity of chyme

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What triggers the gastrocolic reflex and what is its effect?
back: Stomach distension triggers it, leading to increased colonic motility (specifically sigmoid colon contraction)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In which group is the gastrocolic reflex more pronounced, and what everyday phenomenon does it explain?
back: It is more pronounced in children/babies, and explains the urge to defecate after meals

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What triggers the gastroileal reflex and what is its effect?
back: Stomach distention triggers it, leading to increased ileal peristalsis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What happens to the ileocecal valve during the gastroileal reflex?
back: It relaxes, allowing old ileal contents to move into the colon

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the three steps in the mechanism of the defecation reflex?
back: (a) Rectal distension, (b) relaxation of the internal anal sphincter (involuntary, via parasympathetic system), (c) relaxation of the external anal sphincter (voluntary control)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What rectal pressure corresponds to the first urge to defecate?
back: 18 mmHg

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What rectal pressure corresponds to involuntary defecation?
back: 55 mmHg

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the two broad types of GI motility?
back: Electrical motility and Mechanical motility

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What generates the Basal Electrical Rhythm (BER) and what is its voltage range?
back: It is generated by the interstitial cells of Cajal (the GI pacemaker cells), ranging from -45 to -65 mV

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Does the Basal Electrical Rhythm (BER) itself cause contraction?
back: No â BER does not cause contraction; it is a pre-contraction potential that is present all the time

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is a spike potential and when does it occur?
back: A potential that causes contraction; it only occurs when the smooth muscle is excited (regulates the strength/movement of contraction)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In which region of the gut is BER-driven contractility maximum, and which segment is highest within it?
back: Contractility is maximum in the small intestine, with the order Duodenum > Jejunum > Ileum

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In which region of the gut is BER-driven contractility minimum, and which segment is lowest within it?
back: Contractility is minimum in the large intestine and stomach, with the order Caecum < Stomach < Sigmoid

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the approximate BER frequency (cycles/min) for the stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, and sigmoid colon?
back: Stomach 4/min, Duodenum 12/min (maximum), Jejunum 11/min, Ileum 8/min, Cecum 2/min (minimum), Sigmoid 6/min

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does acetylcholine (parasympathetic) affect intestinal spike potentials and motility?
back: It increases spike potentials and increases intestinal contractions and motility

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does epinephrine (sympathetic) affect intestinal spike potentials and motility?
back: It decreases spike potentials and decreases intestinal contractions and motility

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the two types of mechanical motility seen in the fed state?
back: Segmentation (churning of food) and Peristalsis (pushes food forward)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which neurotransmitters mediate contraction during peristalsis?
back: Acetylcholine (ACh) and Substance P

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which neurotransmitters mediate relaxation during peristalsis?
back: VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide) and NO (Nitric Oxide)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What condition results when VIP fails to relax the smooth muscle (e.g. at the lower esophageal sphincter)?
back: Achalasia

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the Migratory Motor Complex (MMC) and in what state does it occur?
back: A pattern of mechanical motility occurring in the fasting state, also called 'housekeeping waves', that sweeps through the intestine to clear residual food

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How long after food intake does the MMC begin, and what triggers it?
back: 90â120 minutes after food intake; it is triggered by hunger

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which hormone mediates the MMC, and what class of drugs acts as agonists of this hormone?
back: Motilin mediates the MMC; macrolide antibiotics act as motilin agonists (used clinically as prokinetics)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What happens to motilin levels after eating?
back: Motilin levels decrease after eating (negative feedback)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: At what speed does the MMC travel through the gut?
back: 5 cm/min

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the three phases of the Migratory Motor Complex?
back: Phase I, Phase II, and Phase III (occurring cyclically, about 90 minutes apart from the last meal, ending when a meal is taken)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which cells secrete gastrin and where are they located?
back: G cells, located in the antrum and duodenum

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the most potent stimulus for gastrin release?
back: GRP (Gastrin Releasing Peptide) released from the Vagus nerve

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the main actions of gastrin?
back: Increased gastric acid secretion and increased gastric motility

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In which three conditions is gastrin increased?
back: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (due to gastrinoma, the most common pancreatic NET), chronic atrophic gastritis, and chronic PPI therapy

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Besides GRP, what other stimuli increase gastrin release?
back: Stomach distention and amino acids (in addition to vagal stimulation via GRP)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What inhibits gastrin release?
back: A gastric pH below 1.5 (acid negative feedback acting via parietal cells)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which cells secrete CCK (cholecystokinin) and where?
back: I cells, located in the antrum and small intestine

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the main actions of CCK?
back: Increased pancreatic exocrine (enzyme) secretion, increased gallbladder contraction (cholagogue effect), decreased gastric emptying, and increased sphincter of Oddi relaxation

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What stimulates CCK release?
back: Fatty acids and amino acids

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Through what pathway does CCK cause pancreatic secretion?
back: It acts on neural muscarinic pathways to cause pancreatic secretion

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which cells secrete secretin and where?
back: S cells, located in the duodenum

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the main actions of secretin?
back: Increased pancreatic HCO3- secretion, decreased gastric acid secretion, and increased bile secretion (a choleretic effect)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What stimulates secretin release?
back: Acid and fatty acids in the lumen of the duodenum

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Why is secretin-driven HCO3- secretion functionally important?
back: The HCO3- neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum, which allows pancreatic enzymes to function properly

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the strongest choleretic agents?
back: Bile salts

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which cells secrete somatostatin and where?
back: D cells, located in the pancreatic islets and stomach

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Summarize the overall effect of somatostatin on the GI tract.
back: It 'slows down everything' â decreases gastric acid and pepsinogen secretion, decreases pancreatic and small intestinal fluid secretion, decreases gallbladder contraction, and decreases insulin and glucagon release

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What regulates somatostatin secretion?
back: Increased by acid; decreased by vagal stimulation

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the somatostatin analogue drug and its clinical uses.
back: Octreotide â used to treat acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma, and variceal bleeding

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is a notable side effect of somatostatin/octreotide therapy?
back: Gallstones, due to gallbladder stasis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which cells secrete GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide, aka gastric inhibitory peptide) and where?
back: K cells, located in the duodenum and jejunum

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the exocrine and endocrine actions of GIP?
back: Exocrine: decreased gastric H+ secretion. Endocrine: increased insulin release

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What stimulates GIP release?
back: Fatty acids, amino acids, and oral glucose

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Explain the 'incretin effect'.
back: Oral glucose produces a greater insulin response than an equivalent intravenous glucose dose, because oral glucose additionally triggers GIP (and GLP-1) secretion from the gut

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name a GLP-1 analogue drug mentioned as an example.
back: Semaglutide

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the source of VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide)?
back: Enteric/parasympathetic neurons found in sphincters, the gallbladder, and the small intestine

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the main actions of VIP?
back: Increased intestinal water and electrolyte secretion, and increased relaxation of intestinal smooth muscle and sphincters

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What regulates VIP secretion?
back: Increased by distention and vagal stimulation; decreased by adrenergic (sympathetic) input

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is a VIPoma and what syndrome does it cause?
back: A VIP-secreting tumour causing WDHA syndrome â Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria (due to inhibition of gastric acid)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is ghrelin's source and main action?
back: Secreted by the stomach; it increases appetite

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What regulates ghrelin secretion?
back: Increased in the fasting state; suppressed by food intake

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does ghrelin level change in Prader-Willi syndrome versus after gastric bypass surgery?
back: Increased in Prader-Willi syndrome; decreased after gastric bypass surgery

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: According to CoreBTR, how does small intestine secretion volume compare to the stomach's, and is there a source discrepancy?
back: CoreBTR (the updated/authoritative source) states maximum secretion is Small Intestine > Stomach; note the Btr 2.0 notes state maximum secretion is at the stomach â CoreBTR should be followed as it is the newer source

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the approximate total daily volume of all GI secretions?
back: About 7 litres per day

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which GI segment produces the most alkaline secretion, and which glands are responsible?
back: The duodenum, via Brunner's glands

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which GI segment produces the most acidic secretion, and what is its approximate pH?
back: The stomach, with an approximate pH of 1.5

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Where is K+ concentration maximum among GI secretions?
back: In the colon

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Where is the maximum total amount of K+ secreted?
back: In the salivary glands

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Where is Na+ concentration at its minimum among GI secretions?
back: In the salivary glands

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Describe the two-step process of saliva formation.
back: Primary secretion occurs from acinar cells; in the ducts this is modified â Na+ is actively reabsorbed, Cl- is passively reabsorbed, while K+ is actively secreted and HCO3- is passively secreted, giving final saliva that is low in NaCl and has secreted K+/HCO3-

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does pancreatic juice electrolyte composition change with flow rate?
back: HCO3- concentration rises steeply as flow rate increases, while Na+ and K+ remain roughly constant, and Cl- falls reciprocally to HCO3-

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does gastric juice electrolyte composition change with secretory flow rate?
back: H+ and Cl- concentrations are high and increase with flow rate, while Na+ and K+ concentrations are low

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does saliva electrolyte composition change with flow rate?
back: Na+ and HCO3- concentrations increase as salivary flow rate increases

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the anatomical regions of the stomach, and where does H. pylori characteristically reside?
back: Cardia, fundus, body, antrum, and pylorus; H. pylori characteristically resides in the antrum

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which region of the stomach mucosa has mucus-producing cells predominating?
back: The fundus

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Describe the layers of a gastric gland from the isthmus to the base.
back: Isthmus (contains stem cells for epithelial regeneration) â Neck (mucous neck cells, aka foveolar cells) â Neck/upper gland (parietal/oxyntic cells) â Base of gland (chief/peptic cells)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What do parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete?
back: HCl and intrinsic factor

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What do chief (peptic) cells secrete?
back: The zymogen pepsinogen

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is MÃ©nÃ©trier disease and its key features?
back: A condition of foveolar cell hyperplasia, producing giant gastric folds and protein loss

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What gastric histologic change occurs in gastrinoma?
back: Parietal cell hypertrophy due to excess gastrin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What causes pernicious anemia at the level of the stomach, and its consequence?
back: Decrease/destruction of parietal cells, leading to low intrinsic factor and resulting Vitamin B12 deficiency

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the three phases of gastric acid production with their approximate contribution.
back: Cephalic phase â anticipatory release (30%); Gastric phase â due to distention (60%); Intestinal phase (10%)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Outline the mechanism of gastric acid production beginning with the vagus nerve.
back: Vagus nerve releases GRP (Gastrin Releasing Peptide) â stimulates G cells to release Gastrin â Gastrin stimulates ECL-like cells to release Histamine â Histamine activates Parietal cells â Parietal cells produce HCl and Intrinsic Factor

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What inhibits GRP release, thereby limiting gastric acid production?
back: Somatostatin, released from D cells

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Besides histamine, what else do ECL cells in the fundus secrete?
back: Mucus and trefoil peptide

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the 'alkaline tide' phenomenon?
back: A rise in blood pH that occurs after gastric acid secretion (e.g. after meals or vomiting), reflecting HCO3- release into the blood as H+ is secreted into the gastric lumen

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the purpose of the Schilling test?
back: To localize the cause of Vitamin B12 malabsorption using radioactive B12

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Describe Step 1 of the Schilling test and its normal result.
back: Oral radioactive B12 is given together with an IM (non-radioactive) vitamin B12 dose to saturate B12-binding receptors/transport proteins; normally more than 10% of the radioactive B12 appears in urine

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: If Step 1 of the Schilling test shows <10% radioactive B12 in urine, what should be suspected, and what is done next?
back: Malabsorption is present (or dietary deficiency, e.g. in vegans); the test is repeated with intrinsic factor added

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In the Schilling test, what does normalization after adding intrinsic factor (Step 2) indicate?
back: Pernicious anemia (lack of endogenous intrinsic factor was the cause)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In the Schilling test, what does normalization after adding antibiotics (Step 3) indicate?
back: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO/BOGS), for example due to strictures or diabetes mellitus

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In the Schilling test, what does normalization after adding pancreatic enzymes (Step 4) indicate?
back: Pancreatitis (pancreatic enzyme insufficiency was the cause)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In the Schilling test, if the result remains abnormal even after adding pancreatic enzymes, what is suspected?
back: A mucosal defect at the ileum, such as Celiac disease, Tropical sprue, or Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) infection

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the mechanism of M1 blockers such as Pirenzepine/Telenzepine?
back: They reduce vagal stimulation of parietal cells

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the prostaglandin analogue used for acid suppression, and its most specific indication?
back: Misoprostol; it is the most specific treatment for NSAID-induced ulcers (though PPIs remain the overall drug of choice)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Why do NSAIDs predispose to peptic ulcers?
back: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, and prostaglandins normally provide protective effects on the gastric mucosa

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the three PPIs listed.
back: Pantoprazole, Omeprazole, and Lansoprazole

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Why are PPIs called 'hit and run' drugs?
back: Because they irreversibly destroy proton pumps, so their effect lasts beyond the drug's own plasma half-life

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which drug class is the overall drug of choice for acid suppression?
back: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List five side effects of PPIs.
back: C. difficile infection (pseudomembranous colitis), Vitamin B12 deficiency (since intrinsic factor needs an acidic environment for activation), allergic interstitial nephritis (with eosinophilia), pneumonia, and Ca2+/Mg2+ deficiency (increasing fracture risk)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the specific side effect of omeprazole, and its clinical consequence?
back: Omeprazole is a CYP2C19 inhibitor, an enzyme required to activate clopidogrel; co-administration risks therapeutic failure of clopidogrel

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: When should PPIs ideally be taken relative to meals?
back: About 30 minutes before a meal

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is Vonoprazan and how does it work?
back: A newer acid-suppressant drug that reversibly blocks the proton pump by binding to its potassium-binding site

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the three H2 blockers mentioned.
back: Cimetidine, Famotidine, and Nizatidine

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the notable side effects of cimetidine?
back: CYP enzyme inhibition and gynecomastia

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What distinguishes lafutidine, a newer H2 blocker?
back: It releases nitric oxide, causing vasodilation, which gives it an additional ulceroprotective effect

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the two components of a common antacid combination, and their opposite bowel side effects?
back: Al(OH)3 (causes constipation) and Mg(OH)2 (causes diarrhea) â mnemonic 'Mg - Makes you Go'

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What syndrome can excess CaCO3 antacid use cause, and what is its triad?
back: Milk-alkali syndrome (from increased HCO3- absorption): metabolic alkalosis, hypercalcemia (excess calcium reabsorption in the distal nephron), and acute kidney injury

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does the onset of relief compare between antacids and PPIs?
back: Antacids give immediate relief, whereas PPIs take longer to act

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the two ulceroprotective drugs and their mechanism.
back: Sucralfate and Bismuth; they form a protective coat over the ulcer (partly by increasing mucus)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How should other medications be timed relative to ulceroprotective agents like sucralfate/bismuth?
back: They should be spaced 120 minutes (2 hours) apart

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What characteristic side effect occurs with bismuth?
back: Black discoloration of the tongue (and stomach)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the Triple Therapy (CAP regimen) for H. pylori eradication?
back: Clarithromycin + Amoxicillin + PPI

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the Quadruple Therapy for H. pylori eradication, and its mnemonic?
back: Bismuth + Metronidazole + Tetracycline + PPI â mnemonic 'BMT + PPI'

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the bulk-forming laxative discussed.
back: Methylcellulose

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the two osmotic laxatives, and which is the drug of choice for IBS-C?
back: Lactulose and PEG (polyethylene glycol); PEG is the drug of choice for constipation-predominant IBS (IBS-C)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What additional therapeutic use does lactulose have, and how does it work?
back: It is used in hepatic encephalopathy; it is converted to lactic acid in an acidic colonic environment, which converts ammonia (NH3) to ammonium (NH4+), reducing ammonia absorption

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the stimulant laxatives and their characteristic side effect.
back: Senna (side effect: melanosis coli) and Bisacodyl

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the Cl- channel activator laxative.
back: Lubiprostone

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the Guanylate Cyclase agonist laxatives and their mechanism.
back: Linaclotide and Plecanatide; they raise cGMP, which activates CFTR

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the 5-HT4 agonist used for constipation.
back: Prucalopride

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the NHE3 inhibitor laxative and its mechanism.
back: Tenapanor; it inhibits the intestinal Na+-H+ exchanger, increasing Na+ excretion and consequently increasing H2O excretion into the stool

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What drug class treats opioid-induced constipation and post-op ileus, and name three examples.
back: Peripheral opioid receptor inhibitors (that do not cross the blood-brain barrier): Alvimopan, Naloxegol, and Methylnaltrexone

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which common GI side effect of opioids (e.g. morphine) is exploited therapeutically in diarrhea treatment?
back: Constipation â since opioid mu-receptor agonism decreases intestinal motility

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which enzyme normally metabolizes endogenous opioids, and what drug class inhibits it to treat secretory diarrhea?
back: Enkephalinase; Enkephalinase inhibitors (such as Racecadotril) enhance endogenous opioid action and are used to treat secretory diarrhea

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is Racecadotril used to treat?
back: Secretory diarrhea

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which mu-opioid agonist is the drug of choice for IBS-D, and what is a key caution with its use?
back: Loperamide; it should be avoided in infectious diarrhea

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is diphenoxylate combined with, and why?
back: It is combined with Atropine; the atropine is added specifically to discourage/prevent misuse of diphenoxylate (via unpleasant anticholinergic effects)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the 5-HT3 antagonist used for diarrhea and its effect.
back: Alosetron; it decreases intestinal motility and visceral pain

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name three bile acid binding resins and their diarrhea indication.
back: Colesevelam, Colestipol, and Cholestyramine; they reduce bile-acid-induced diarrhea

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the direct spasmolytic drugs used for abdominal cramps in IBS.
back: Mebeverine and Dicycloverine (Dicyclomine)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Summarize the Rome IV '1-2-3' criteria for diagnosing IBS.
back: Recurrent abdominal pain for at least 1 day/week on average over the last 3 months, associated with 2 or more of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, or change in stool form; with symptom onset at least 6 months prior to diagnosis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Once IBS diagnostic criteria are met, how is the subtype classified using the Bristol Stool Chart?
back: IBS-D (diarrhea-predominant, Bristol type 5 or 6), IBS-C (constipation-predominant, Bristol type 1 or 2), or IBS-M (mixed, Bristol type 1-2 and 5-6)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What red-flag finding argues against a diagnosis of IBS on Rome IV assessment?
back: Presence of blood in the stool

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which fecal markers help distinguish IBD from IBS, and how?
back: Fecal lactoferrin and fecal calprotectin are positive in IBD but not in IBS

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What dietary intervention is recommended for IBS, and what symptoms does it target?
back: A Low FODMAP diet; it helps reduce bloating, abdominal pain, and diarrhea in IBS

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Name the two 5-HT3 blockers ('setrons') discussed, and compare their duration/potency.
back: Ondansetron (shortest acting) and Palonosetron (longest acting, most potent)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: What are the drug-of-choice indications for 5-HT3 blockers?
back: Post-chemotherapy N&V, post-operative N&V, post-radiotherapy N&V, and nausea/vomiting of pregnancy

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: List the side effects of 5-HT3 blockers.
back: QT prolongation, headache, and constipation

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: For cisplatin-induced nausea/vomiting, which phase (early or delayed) do 5-HT3 blockers primarily cover?
back: The early-onset phase (5-HT3 blockade covers early cisplatin-induced N&V, while NK-1 inhibitors cover the delayed phase)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Name the NK-1/Substance P inhibitor antiemetic and its main indication.
back: Aprepitant; it is the drug of choice for cisplatin-induced delayed nausea and vomiting

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Name the CB1 receptor agonist (cannabinoid) antiemetics and their notable side effects.
back: Dronabinol and Nabilone; side effects include red eyes and decreased blood pressure

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: What is the drug of choice for morning sickness of pregnancy, and what is the general management principle in pregnancy?
back: Doxylamine + Vitamin B6; initial management of nausea in pregnancy is always conservative

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: What is the drug of choice for sea sickness (nausea from motion on water), and its drug class?
back: Meclizine or Dimenhydrinate, both antihistamines

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: What is the drug of choice for motion sickness from general movement (car, plane, amusement rides)?
back: Scopolamine transdermal patch (also known as hyoscine)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: What is the drug of choice for mountain (high-altitude) sickness, and its drug class?
back: Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: By what mechanism does acetazolamide help in mountain sickness?
back: It causes a mild metabolic acidosis (via bicarbonate diuresis) that stimulates hyperventilation, promoting CO2 washout and improving oxygenation at altitude

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Name the two D2 blocker prokinetic drugs, and state which one crosses the blood-brain barrier.
back: Metoclopramide (crosses the BBB) and Domperidone (does not cross the BBB)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: What adverse effects result from metoclopramide crossing the blood-brain barrier?
back: Extrapyramidal symptoms (via the nigrostriatal pathway) and increased prolactin (via the tuberoinfundibular pathway)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Which D2 blocker prokinetic is generally more preferred, and why?
back: Domperidone, because it does not cross the blood-brain barrier and therefore has fewer CNS side effects

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: In which motility disorder is the 5-HT4 agonist class of prokinetics particularly useful?
back: Gastroparesis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Name the 5-HT4 agonist prokinetic drugs.
back: Mosapride and Prucalopride

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Name the CCK antagonist prokinetic drug.
back: Dexloxiglumide

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Name the motilin agonist prokinetic drug.
back: Erythromycin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Compare the location affected by H. pylori-associated gastritis versus autoimmune gastritis.
back: H. pylori-associated gastritis affects the antrum; autoimmune gastritis affects the body of the stomach

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Compare gastric acid production in H. pylori-associated gastritis versus autoimmune gastritis.
back: H. pylori gastritis: increased to slightly decreased acid production. Autoimmune gastritis: markedly decreased acid production

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Compare serum gastrin levels in H. pylori-associated gastritis versus autoimmune gastritis.
back: H. pylori gastritis: normal to markedly increased gastrin. Autoimmune gastritis: markedly increased gastrin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
deck: Part-5: Vomiting, Motion Sickness & Gastritis Types
front: Compare the associated risks of H. pylori-associated gastritis versus autoimmune gastritis.
back: H. pylori gastritis: adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, and affects lower socioeconomic status. Autoimmune gastritis: mucosal atrophy, adenocarcinoma, and carcinoid tumor (linked to pernicious anemia)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the formula for the Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG)?
back: SAAG = Serum albumin â Ascites albumin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What SAAG value indicates the presence of portal hypertension?
back: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or higher (High SAAG)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What SAAG value excludes portal hypertension as the cause of ascites?
back: A SAAG below 1.1 g/dL (Low SAAG)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In high-SAAG ascites, what does an ascitic protein below 2.5 g/dL indicate?
back: Liver cirrhosis â the diseased liver is unable to produce sufficient albumin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In high-SAAG ascites, what does an ascitic protein of 2.5 g/dL or higher indicate, and name three causes to consider?
back: The liver is functioning normally, and the cause of portal hypertension is extrahepatic: Budd-Chiari syndrome, Constrictive pericarditis, or IVC obstruction

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In low-SAAG ascites, what does the presence of frothy urine suggest as the cause?
back: Nephrotic syndrome

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In low-SAAG ascites, what do fever and weight loss suggest as the cause?
back: Tuberculosis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In low-SAAG ascites, what does weight loss in an elderly patient suggest as the cause?
back: Malignancy

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In low-SAAG ascites, what does acute abdominal pain suggest as the cause?
back: Pancreatitis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What minimum volume of ascitic fluid is needed for detection on ultrasound?

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What minimum volume of ascitic fluid produces clinically detectable shifting dullness?
back: 500 mL

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What minimum volume of ascitic fluid produces a detectable fluid thrill?

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How is mild ascites (detectable only on USG, no clinical features) managed?
back: Salt restriction

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How is moderate ascites (with clinical features present) managed?
back: Furosemide followed by Spironolactone or Eplerenone (eplerenone is preferred if gynecomastia occurs with spironolactone)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How is severe ascites (with respiratory distress) managed?
back: High-volume paracentesis (4â5 L), with albumin supplementation if more than 2.5 L of fluid is removed

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the general guideline for albumin replacement during large-volume paracentesis?
back: Approximately 6â8 g of albumin per litre of ascitic fluid removed, given to prevent post-paracentesis fluid shifts

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What clinical presentation should raise suspicion for Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
back: Ascites accompanied by fever

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What ascitic fluid neutrophil count is diagnostic of SBP?
back: Greater than 250 cells/mm3

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the most common causative organism of SBP?
back: Gram-negative bacteria, most commonly E. coli

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the drug of choice for treating SBP?
back: Third-generation cephalosporins (e.g. ceftriaxone or cefotaxime)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Besides antibiotics, what additional intervention improves survival in SBP?
back: Albumin infusion

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How is chronic diarrhea defined by duration?
back: Diarrhea lasting more than 1 month

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the first investigation to order in chronic diarrhea, and its formula?
back: The stool osmotic gap: Stool osmotic gap = 290 â 2 Ã (stool Na + stool K)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What stool osmotic gap value indicates osmotic diarrhea, and how does it behave with fasting?
back: A high gap (>50 mOsm/kg) indicates osmotic diarrhea, which characteristically improves/resolves on fasting

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What stool osmotic gap value indicates secretory diarrhea?
back: A low gap (<50 mOsm/kg) indicates secretory diarrhea

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List three causes of secretory (low osmotic gap) chronic diarrhea.
back: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), Carcinoid syndrome, and VIPoma

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In osmotic diarrhea, what test is done next, and what does a positive result indicate?
back: The hydrogen breath test; a positive result indicates lactose intolerance

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: If the hydrogen breath test is negative in osmotic diarrhea workup, what is checked next, and what cutoff defines steatorrhea?
back: Stool fat is checked; stool fat greater than 7% defines steatorrhea, indicating malabsorption

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Once malabsorption/steatorrhea is confirmed, which test helps localize the defect to the pancreas versus the intestine?
back: The D-xylose test, which measures how well the intestine absorbs D-xylose

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What does a normal D-xylose test suggest in a steatorrhea workup, and what confirms the diagnosis?
back: It suggests pancreatitis/pancreatic insufficiency (the intestine itself is normal); a fecal elastase test is done to confirm pancreatic insufficiency

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What does an abnormal D-xylose test suggest, and what is the next step?
back: It suggests the intestine itself is abnormal; a 7-day trial of Rifaximin is given

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: If diarrhea improves after a Rifaximin trial, what is the diagnosis?
back: BOGS/SIBO â Bacterial Overgrowth Syndrome / Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: If there is no improvement after the Rifaximin trial, what is suspected and what investigation follows?
back: Mucosal disease is suspected, and a biopsy of the intestinal mucosa is performed

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: On mucosal biopsy in chronic malabsorptive diarrhea, what finding points to Celiac sprue?
back: Flattening of villi with crypt hyperplasia

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: On mucosal biopsy in chronic malabsorptive diarrhea, what finding points to Whipple's disease?
back: PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What organism classically causes acute diarrhea (<6 hours) after eating reheated/fried rice (Chinese food), and by what mechanism?
back: Bacillus cereus, via an emetic-type illness caused by a preformed toxin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What organism classically causes acute diarrhea (<6 hours) from dairy products?
back: Staphylococcus aureus (via preformed toxin)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What organism causes traveler's diarrhea, and what toxins does it produce?
back: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC); its heat-labile (LT) toxin increases cAMP, and its heat-stable (ST) toxin increases cGMP

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism produces classic 'rice water' stools?
back: Vibrio cholerae

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism, linked to shellfish ingestion, causes diarrhea, and what toxin is it associated with?
back: Vibrio parahaemolyticus, associated with the Kanagawa toxin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism causes diarrhea associated with camping/contaminated water, presenting with malabsorption?
back: Giardia (lamblia)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism causes acute right iliac fossa pain mimicking appendicitis?
back: Yersinia enterocolitica

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism causes diarrhea after heavy antibiotic use?
back: Clostridioides (Clostridium) difficile

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism causes bloody diarrhea associated with contaminated poultry and eggs?
back: Salmonella

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism causes bloody diarrhea with severe dehydration?
back: Shigella

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism is linked to bloody diarrhea followed by Guillain-BarrÃ© syndrome or reactive (Reiter's) arthritis?
back: Campylobacter

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism causes bloody diarrhea complicated by uremia and hemolytic anemia?
back: EHEC (enterohemorrhagic E. coli) serotype O157:H7, causing Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism produces flask-shaped ulcers, and what is its tissue-damaging mechanism?
back: Entamoeba histolytica (amebic infection); damage occurs via erythrophagocytosis (ingestion of red blood cells)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism/condition causes longitudinal intestinal ulcers?
back: Salmonella typhi (typhoid)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which organism/condition causes transverse intestinal ulcers?
back: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (intestinal TB)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the immunological basis of celiac sprue?
back: Cell-mediated immunity directed against gliadin, a component of gluten

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which HLA types are associated with celiac disease?
back: HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which segment of the small intestine is characteristically affected in celiac disease, and what nutritional deficiency results?
back: The duodenum is affected, causing impaired iron absorption and iron deficiency

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What two conditions are celiac disease patients at increased risk of developing?
back: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, and Dermatitis herpetiformis (treated with Dapsone)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the best screening test for celiac disease?
back: TTG IgA (Tissue Transglutaminase Antibody)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name two other antibody tests used in celiac disease and their limitation.
back: Endomysial antibody (EMA-IgA); and Anti-Gliadin antibody, which has low specificity and sensitivity

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What unusual dermatoglyphic finding is associated with celiac disease?
back: Loss of fingerprints

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the key differential diagnosis for celiac disease, and how does its etiology differ?
back: Tropical sprue, which has an infective etiology (unlike celiac disease's gluten-mediated autoimmune etiology)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What classification system, applied to duodenal biopsy, is the gold standard for diagnosing celiac disease?
back: The Marsh classification

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What dietary restriction is advised in celiac disease, using the mnemonic BROW?
back: Avoid Barley, Rye, Oats, and Wheat (Rice and Maize are permitted)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Outline the pathogenesis of celiac disease from gluten ingestion to tissue damage.
back: Dietary gliadin is deamidated by tissue transglutaminase (tTG); deamidated gliadin binds HLA-DQ2/DQ8 on antigen-presenting cells, activating CD4+ T cells; these secrete IFN-gamma and induce epithelial cells to produce IL-15, which activates CD8+ intraepithelial T cells (via NKG2D-MIC-A interaction) causing tissue damage; activated CD4+ T cells also help B cells produce anti-gliadin, anti-endomysial, and anti-tTG antibodies

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What histological changes are seen on duodenal biopsy in celiac disease?
back: Villous atrophy, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, increased mitosis, and crypt elongation (crypt hyperplasia)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What organism causes Whipple disease?
back: Tropheryma whipplei, a Gram-positive bacterium

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the core mechanism of malabsorption in Whipple disease?
back: Impairment of lymphatic transport

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Summarize the 'CAN' mnemonic for the systemic features of Whipple disease.
back: Cardiac involvement, Arthralgia, and Neurological involvement (dementia, oculomasticatory myorhythmia)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is oculomasticatory myorhythmia, and what is its clinical significance?
back: A rhythmic eye and jaw movement that is characteristic (pathognomonic) of Whipple's disease

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which CNS manifestation of Whipple disease is most common, and what is the prognostic significance of CNS involvement?
back: Dementia is the most common CNS manifestation; CNS involvement carries a poor prognosis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is an important differential diagnosis for Whipple disease on biopsy, and how are the two distinguished?
back: Gastric TB, which also shows foamy macrophages; TB shows AFB positivity while Whipple's disease shows PAS positivity

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the treatment regimen for Whipple disease?
back: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily for 2 weeks, followed by long-term oral therapy with TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) twice daily

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the two broad categories of colonic polyps?
back: Non-neoplastic and Neoplastic

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the three types of non-neoplastic polyps.
back: Hyperplastic polyps, Inflammatory polyps, and Hamartomatous polyps

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which type of non-neoplastic polyp is the most common?
back: Hyperplastic polyps

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What causes hyperplastic polyps?
back: They are noncancerous growths in the digestive tract resulting from overproduction of cells

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the histological hallmark of a hyperplastic polyp?
back: Serrations confined to the superficial 1/3 of the gland/crypt

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: If serrations are seen throughout the full thickness of the crypt rather than only superficially, what diagnosis should be considered?
back: A Serrated Sessile Adenoma (SSA), rather than a simple hyperplastic polyp

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What clinical presentation is characteristic of an inflammatory polyp, and what syndrome is it also known as?
back: History of bleeding and mucus discharge; also known as Solitary Rectal Ulcer Syndrome (SRUS)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: A 4-year-old presents with rectal bleeding and a hamartomatous polyp containing many cystic spaces. What is the diagnosis and implicated gene?
back: Juvenile polyposis syndrome; caused by mutation of the SMAD4 gene

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What extraintestinal association is seen with juvenile polyposis syndrome?
back: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (AVM)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: An 11-year-old presents with intussusception (the polyp acting as a lead point) and a hamartomatous polyp with an arborising (tree-like) pattern. What is the diagnosis and implicated gene?
back: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome; caused by mutation of the STK11 (aka LKB-1) gene

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What mucocutaneous finding is characteristic of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome?
back: Mucosal (cutaneous) pigmentation

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which malignancy carries the highest (near 100%) lifetime risk in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome?
back: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Besides pancreatic cancer, which other cancers have increased risk in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome?
back: Colon, stomach, small intestine, breast, thyroid, lung, and gonadal (sex-cord/stromal cell) cancers

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the two histological subtypes of adenomatous (neoplastic) polyps, and which carries a worse prognosis?
back: Tubular type and Villous type; the Villous type has a poorer prognosis ('villous = villain') and requires ruling out colon cancer

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the single most important prognostic marker for an adenomatous polyp?
back: Its size

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Briefly describe the Haggit classification and its clinical use.
back: A histological staging system (Levels 0â4) for depth of invasion of a malignant colonic polyp, used mainly for pedunculated adenomas; deeper invasion (especially Level 4, invasion into the bowel wall submucosa beyond the polyp stalk) carries a worse prognosis, and sessile adenomas are considered higher risk since they lack a protective stalk

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is Cowden syndrome â its mutated gene, chromosome, and cancer risk?
back: A hamartomatous polyposis syndrome due to a PTEN mutation on chromosome 10; associated with increased risk of Breast, Endometrial, and Thyroid cancers (mnemonic 'BET')

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What benign skin lesion is associated with Cowden syndrome?
back: Trichilemmoma (a benign tumor arising from hair follicle epithelium)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the key features of Cronkhite-Canada syndrome?
back: A non-hereditary (sporadic) hamartomatous polyposis syndrome associated with ectodermal dysplasia

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In Tuberous Sclerosis-related hamartomatous polyposis, which chromosomes and proteins are involved?
back: Chromosome 9 and 16 mutations, affecting the proteins Hamartin and Tuberin, causing hamartomas in multiple organs

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome associated with?
back: Macrocephaly and developmental delay, along with hamartomatous polyps

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What chromosome and inheritance pattern are associated with Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)?
back: Chromosome 5q, with Autosomal Dominant (AD) transmission

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the lifetime risk of colon cancer in FAP, and by what age does it typically develop?
back: 100% chance of colon cancer, typically developing by puberty

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which side of the colon is characteristically affected by FAP-associated cancer, and what complication commonly results?
back: Left-sided colon cancer, commonly causing obstruction

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Outline the adenoma-carcinoma sequence of gene mutations, using the mnemonic 'AK-53'.
back: Normal mucosa â APC mutation (chromosome 5) â Early adenoma â K-RAS mutation (chromosome 12) â Late adenoma â p53 mutation (chromosome 17) â Adenocarcinoma. Mnemonic 'AK-53': A (APC), K (K-RAS), 53 (p53) â the '53' refers to the p53 gene's name, not a sum of the chromosome numbers

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Besides APC, K-RAS, and p53, what other genetic event is involved in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence?
back: Loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at 18q21, involving SMAD2 and SMAD4, along with telomerase and other cancer genes

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What malignancy of the pancreas is FAP syndrome associated with, and its classic presentation?
back: Ampullary cancer of the pancreas, presenting with waxing and waning jaundice

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the two syndromes associated with FAP, and their mnemonics?
back: Gardner's syndrome (mnemonic 'Garden of tumors') and Turcot syndrome (mnemonic 'Turban: Tumors in head')

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the features of Gardner's syndrome.
back: Supernumerary teeth, Osteoma, Fibromas, and Congenital Hypertrophy of Retinal Pigment Epithelium (CHRPE)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the features of Turcot syndrome.
back: Medulloblastoma (with drop metastases) and Glioblastoma multiforme

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the underlying defect, inheritance pattern, and mutated gene in MUTYH-Associated Polyposis (MAP)?
back: A base excision repair defect, inherited in an Autosomal Recessive pattern, due to mutation of the MUTYH gene

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How many adenomatous polyps are typically seen in MUTYH-Associated Polyposis, and what can develop later?
back: Usually fewer than 100 adenomatous polyps; duodenal adenomas can develop later

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which cancers (besides colorectal) is MUTYH-Associated Polyposis linked to?
back: Ovarian and bladder cancers

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What colonoscopic surveillance schedule is recommended for FAP (APC-linked)?
back: Starting at age 10â12 years, repeated every 1â2 years

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What colonoscopic surveillance schedule is recommended for MUTYH-Associated Polyposis?
back: Starting at age 20â25 years, repeated every 1â2 years

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What definitive surgical treatment is used for FAP, and what reconstructive procedure typically accompanies it?
back: Total proctocolectomy, typically with IPAA (Ileal Pouch-Anal Anastomosis)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Is Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC/Lynch syndrome) associated with polyps?
back: No â it is not associated with polyps

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the inheritance pattern of HNPCC, and how does its prevalence compare with FAP?
back: Autosomal Dominant (AD); it is more common than FAP

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the lifetime risk of colon cancer in HNPCC?

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which side of the colon is characteristically affected by HNPCC-associated cancer, and its typical presentation?
back: Right-sided colon cancer, presenting with bleeding

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the molecular defect underlying HNPCC, and which two genes are classically implicated?
back: A DNA mismatch repair defect, classically involving the MLH-1 and MSH-2 genes

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the Revised Amsterdam Criteria II for identifying families likely to have Lynch syndrome.
back: At least 3 relatives with an HNPCC-associated cancer (colorectal, endometrial, small bowel, ureter, or renal pelvis); one must be a first-degree relative of the other two; at least 2 successive generations affected; at least 1 diagnosed before age 50 years; Familial Adenomatous Polyposis must be excluded; and the tumor must be confirmed histologically

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In what proportion of melanoma cases is a BRAF mutation found?

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In what proportion of colorectal cancer cases is a BRAF mutation found?

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In what proportion of papillary thyroid carcinoma cases is a BRAF mutation found?

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In what proportion of NSCLC (non-small cell lung cancer) cases is a BRAF mutation found?

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Besides melanoma, colorectal, thyroid, and NSCLC, which two other tumors are associated with BRAF mutation?
back: Hairy cell leukemia and Langerhans cell histiocytosis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which specific BRAF mutation subtype is commonly referenced in these tumors?
back: V600E

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Name the RAF inhibitor drugs used to target BRAF-mutated tumors.
back: Vemurafenib and Dabrafenib

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: In which additional cancer have BRAF inhibitors shown efficacy when the tumor harbors a BRAF mutation?
back: Lung cancer

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are the two major conditions classified under Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)?
back: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What clinical presentation is common to both forms of IBD?
back: Chronic abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and abdominal tenderness

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which fecal markers help distinguish IBD from IBS?
back: Fecal lactoferrin and fecal calprotectin are positive in IBD but not in IBS

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which layer(s) of the bowel wall are affected in ulcerative colitis versus Crohn's disease?
back: Ulcerative colitis affects only the superficial mucosa; Crohn's disease is transmural, involving all bowel wall layers

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which part of the colon is always involved in ulcerative colitis, and how does the disease spread?
back: The rectum is always involved (disease starts there), spreading continuously from the rectum proximally through the rest of the colon

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the most common site of involvement in Crohn's disease, and what deficiency can result?
back: The terminal ileum; this can cause Vitamin B12 deficiency

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does the lesion distribution pattern of Crohn's disease differ from ulcerative colitis?
back: Crohn's disease shows skip lesions (discontinuous involvement), whereas ulcerative colitis shows continuous involvement

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Why are strictures and fistulas more common in Crohn's disease than in ulcerative colitis?
back: Because Crohn's disease is a transmural (granulomatous) condition affecting all bowel wall layers, predisposing to fistula and stricture formation, whereas UC involves only the superficial mucosa

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which antibody is associated with ulcerative colitis?
back: P-ANCA

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which antibody is associated with Crohn's disease?
back: ASCA (Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae Antibody)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the characteristic histopathological finding in ulcerative colitis?
back: Crypt abscess

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the characteristic histopathological finding in Crohn's disease?
back: Non-caseating granuloma

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the earliest imaging finding in ulcerative colitis, and what does it reflect?
back: A lead pipe appearance of the colon, reflecting mucosal granularity and loss of haustrations

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the earliest imaging finding in Crohn's disease, and how does it form?
back: A cobblestone appearance, formed by aphthous ulcers combined with serpentine ulcers

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
topic: UC vs Crohn's - Classification, Risk Factors & Management
front: Which classification system is used to grade ulcerative colitis severity?
back: The Truelove and Witts classification

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
topic: UC vs Crohn's - Classification, Risk Factors & Management
front: Which classification system is used for Crohn's disease, and what three parameters does it assess?
back: The Montreal classification, assessing age at diagnosis, location of the ulcer, and behavior of the disease

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
topic: UC vs Crohn's - Classification, Risk Factors & Management
front: What two factors are protective against ulcerative colitis?
back: Smoking and appendectomy

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
topic: UC vs Crohn's - Classification, Risk Factors & Management
front: What two factors are risk factors for Crohn's disease?
back: Smoking and OCPs (oral contraceptive pills)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
topic: UC vs Crohn's - Classification, Risk Factors & Management
front: Outline the management of mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis (<6 stools/day).
back: 5-ASA drugs (Sulfasalazine/Mesalamine), followed by steroids or biologicals if needed

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
topic: UC vs Crohn's - Classification, Risk Factors & Management
front: Outline the management of severe ulcerative colitis (with perforation or toxic megacolon).
back: Surgery (mucosal proctocolectomy)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
topic: UC vs Crohn's - Classification, Risk Factors & Management
front: Outline the management approach for Crohn's disease, and note the role of surgery.
back: Steroids followed by biologicals; surgery is not routinely done for Crohn's disease, because recurrence is common due to skip lesions

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
topic: UC vs Crohn's - Classification, Risk Factors & Management
front: Which drug is useful in both types of IBD, and what other rheumatologic condition is it also useful for?
back: Ustekinumab; it is also useful in psoriatic arthritis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the peripheral (treatment-responsive) extra-articular manifestations of IBD.
back: Peripheral arthritis (migratory polyarthritis), Erythema nodosum, and Episcleritis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the central/axial (treatment-resistant) extra-articular manifestations of IBD.
back: Axial arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis), Pyoderma gangrenosum, Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC), and Uveitis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which antibody links pyoderma gangrenosum and PSC, and with which type of IBD is that antibody associated?
back: P-ANCA, which is associated with ulcerative colitis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the most common extra-intestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease?
back: Renal stones (specifically calcium oxalate stones)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which type of IBD carries an increased risk of colon cancer?
back: Ulcerative colitis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the 'String sign of Kantor', and what other disease can also produce it?
back: A radiographic sign of a distal ileal stricture in Crohn's disease; the same sign can also be seen in intestinal tuberculosis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the 'Comb sign' on imaging, and what does it indicate?
back: Proliferation of the vasa recta, seen on imaging in active Crohn's disease

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is 'creeping fat', and in which disease is it characteristically seen?
back: Mesenteric fat wrapping around the bowel wall, characteristically seen in Crohn's disease

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are pseudopolyps, and in which disease are they seen?
back: Islands of regenerating mucosa surrounded by ulcerated areas, seen in ulcerative colitis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is Zone 1 of the liver acinus also called, and which conditions/toxins affect it first?
back: The peri-portal zone; affected first in viral hepatitis and cocaine toxicity

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is Zone 2 of the liver acinus, and which toxin selectively affects it?
back: The zone lying between Zone 1 and Zone 3; selectively affected by yellow fever

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is Zone 3 of the liver acinus also called, and which conditions affect it first?
back: The centri-lobular zone; affected first in congestion, hypoxia, and intoxication (e.g. alcohol, rifampicin, paracetamol)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What three structures make up the portal triad?
back: Hepatic artery, Portal vein, and Bile duct

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Where are Ito cells (hepatic stellate cells) located, and what are their two key functions?
back: Located in the space of Disse (between hepatocytes and sinusoids); they store Vitamin A, and are responsible for fibrosis in cirrhosis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What substance is deposited in the space of Disse in amyloidosis?
back: Amyloid

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What types of collagen are deposited during bridging fibrosis in cirrhosis?
back: Type I and Type III collagen

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are Kupffer cells, and where in the liver are they located?
back: The resident macrophages of the liver, located within the sinusoids

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is 'nutmeg liver', and which condition causes it?
back: Centrilobular congestion with peri-portal sparing, seen in congestive heart failure

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the mechanism behind nutmeg liver in heart failure?
back: Backflow of blood from a failing heart causes centrilobular congestion around the central vein, while the peri-portal zone (supplied by the hepatic artery) is relatively spared

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which four physical signs of chronic liver disease result from hyperestrogenism, and why do they occur?
back: Spider angiomas, palmar erythema, testicular atrophy, and gynecomastia; they occur because the diseased liver cannot metabolize estrogen, and reduced hepatic synthesis of sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) leads to increased free estrogen

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What two vascular findings result from portal hypertension in cirrhosis?
back: Esophageal and gastric varices, and Caput medusae (dilated abdominal wall veins)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What two bleeding manifestations are seen in cirrhosis, and their cause?
back: Purpura and Petechiae, due to thrombocytopenia and reduced synthesis of clotting factors

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the neurologic manifestations of cirrhosis.
back: Hepatic encephalopathy and asterixis (flapping tremor)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the gastrointestinal manifestations of cirrhosis.
back: Anorexia, nausea/vomiting, dull abdominal pain, and fetor hepaticus

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the hematologic manifestations of cirrhosis.
back: Thrombocytopenia, anemia, coagulation disorders, and splenomegaly

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the vascular/abdominal manifestations of cirrhosis besides varices.
back: Caput medusae, anorectal varices, ascites, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the reproductive manifestations of cirrhosis.
back: Testicular atrophy, gynecomastia, and amenorrhea

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the metabolic manifestations of cirrhosis.
back: Hyperbilirubinemia and hyponatremia

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the cardiovascular manifestations of cirrhosis.
back: Cardiomyopathy and peripheral edema

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which renal complication is among the systemic manifestations of cirrhosis?
back: Hepatorenal syndrome

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What metabolic abnormality underlies hepatic encephalopathy?
back: Increased ammonia (NH3)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the earliest symptom of hepatic encephalopathy?
back: Altered sleep-wake cycle

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the specific clinical sign of hepatic encephalopathy?
back: Asterixis (flapping tremor)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What characteristic EEG finding is seen in hepatic encephalopathy?
back: A triphasic waveform (delta waves)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What staging system is used to grade hepatic encephalopathy?
back: The West Haven staging system

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does rifaximin help manage hepatic encephalopathy?
back: It decreases gut bacteria, thereby reducing intestinal ammonia production

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: How does lactulose help manage hepatic encephalopathy?
back: It is converted to lactic acid in the colon; the resulting acidic environment converts ammonia (NH3) into ammonium (NH4+), which is then excreted in stool

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Is TIPS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt) safe in a patient with hepatic encephalopathy?
back: No â TIPS is contraindicated in hepatic encephalopathy

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What type of kidney injury does hepatorenal syndrome represent, and what is its characteristic FENA value?
back: An example of pre-renal AKI; FENA is less than 1%

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the drug of choice for hepatorenal syndrome?
back: Terlipressin plus Albumin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the underlying pathophysiology of hepatopulmonary syndrome?
back: Dilated capillaries in the lungs, with blood pooling in the lower lobes

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the classic postural symptom of hepatopulmonary syndrome, and what is it called?
back: Dyspnea that worsens in the upright position, known as platypnea-orthodeoxia

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Why does hepatopulmonary syndrome cause worse hypoxia in the upright position?
back: In the upright position, more blood is directed to the dilated vessels in the lower lobes, which are relatively poorly ventilated, causing greater right-to-left shunting

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the most specific serum marker of alcohol-induced liver disease?
back: GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the typical AST elevation and AST/ALT ratio pattern in alcoholic hepatitis?
back: AST is raised, typically below 400 IU/L, with an AST/ALT ratio greater than 2:1 (AST > ALT)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What characteristic inclusion body is seen on liver histology in alcoholic hepatitis, and what is it composed of?
back: Mallory-Denk bodies, composed of intermediate filaments (cytokeratins 8/18)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What type of steatosis accompanies Mallory-Denk bodies in alcoholic hepatitis?
back: Macrovesicular steatosis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What does the Maddrey Discriminant Function (DF) assess, and what is its formula?
back: It assesses severity and mortality in alcoholic hepatitis; DF = 4.6 x [prothrombin time (patient, sec) minus control prothrombin time (sec)] + serum bilirubin

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What Maddrey DF cutoff indicates severe disease requiring steroid therapy?
back: A score greater than 32

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Compare short-term mortality and steroid indication in non-severe (MDF <32) versus severe (MDF >32) alcoholic hepatitis.
back: Non-severe disease: about 10% short-term mortality, steroids not indicated. Severe disease: 30-60% short-term mortality, steroids indicated

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What score is used to assess response to steroid therapy in alcoholic hepatitis?
back: The Lille score

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the typical ALT/AST pattern and ALT range in acute viral hepatitis?
back: ALT is greater than AST, with ALT typically ranging from 400-4000 IU/L

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What histological findings are seen in acute viral hepatitis, besides inflammation?
back: Portal tract expansion and macrovesicular steatosis

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What are Councilman bodies, and in which viral hepatitis are they characteristically seen?
back: Apoptotic hepatocytes, characteristically seen in acute Hepatitis C

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the characteristic hepatocyte finding in Hepatitis B, and which special stains highlight it?
back: Ground glass hepatocytes; highlighted by Orcein stain and Shikata stain

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is MASH, and what was its older/previous name?
back: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis; previously called Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the characteristic histologic finding in MASH, and what must be absent for the diagnosis?
back: Macrovesicular hepatic steatosis, occurring without significant alcohol intake

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: Which conditions is MASH commonly associated with?
back: Metabolic syndrome, obesity, diabetes, and dyslipidemia

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What is the only FDA-approved drug for MASH (as of 2024), its brand name, and mechanism of action?
back: Resmetirom (brand name Rezdiffra); it is a selective thyroid hormone receptor agonist

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: List the off-label/commonly used drug options for MASH and their mechanisms.
back: Vitamin E (antioxidant); Metformin and Pioglitazone (insulin sensitizers â pioglitazone acts via PPAR-gamma); Liraglutide (GLP-1 agonist); Saroglitazar (dual PPAR-alpha + PPAR-gamma agonist); Lanifibranor (pan-PPAR agonist)

subject: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Systems
front: What autoantibodies characterize Type 1 Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH)?
back: SMA (Smooth Muscle Antibody) and ANA (Antinuclear Antibody)
